claims.summary: nodeTop is a 5-port network-on-chip (NoC) router node that routes incoming messages from any of five directions (East, Local, North, South, West) to any output direction, using a route-then-arbitrate architecture.
claims.subject: nodeTop
claims.explanation: The interface has five symmetric directional ports, each with a drive event, a 51-bit message payload, and a free signal. The internal structure consists of five routeMsg instances (one per input direction) that decode routing, and five arbMsg instances (one per output direction) that arbitrate among the five possible input sources for that output. This matches a classic NoC router design where each input is routed to a set of output requests, and each output arbiter selects one request.

claims.summary: nodeTop receives a message on any of five input ports, routes it to one or more output ports via routeMsg instances, and then arbitrates among competing messages for each output port via arbMsg instances.
claims.subject: 5-port message routing and arbitration
claims.explanation: Each input drive event (i_drive*) is connected to a corresponding routeMsg instance (e.g., eastRouteMsg). The routeMsg instances produce five output drive requests (o_driveEArb, o_driveLArb, etc.) that are connected to the five arbMsg instances. Each arbMsg instance receives drive requests from all five routeMsg instances and selects one to forward as the output drive event (o_drive*). The message payloads follow the same path: input messages go to routeMsg instances, and output messages come from arbMsg instances. The free signals flow in the opposite direction: input free signals go to arbMsg instances, and output free signals come from routeMsg instances.

claims.subject: routeMsg instances (eastRouteMsg, localRouteMsg, northRouteMsg, southRouteMsg, westRouteMsg)
claims.summary: Each routeMsg instance decodes the routing for messages arriving from a specific input direction and generates drive requests for each possible output direction.
claims.explanation: Each routeMsg instance receives an input drive event (i_drive*) and the corresponding message payload (i_*InMsg_51). It produces five output drive requests (o_driveEArb, o_driveLArb, o_driveNArb, o_driveSArb, o_driveWArb) that are connected to the five arbMsg instances. This indicates that the routeMsg decodes the destination from the message and asserts the appropriate output request(s). The routeMsg also produces the output free signal (o_free*) for its input direction.

claims.subject: arbMsg instances (eastArbMsg, localArbMsg, northArbMsg, southArbMsg, westArbMsg)
claims.summary: Each arbMsg instance arbitrates among up to five incoming drive requests (one from each routeMsg) for a specific output direction and selects one to forward as the output drive event.
claims.explanation: Each arbMsg instance receives five drive requests (i_driveEast, i_driveLocal, i_driveNorth, i_driveSouth, i_driveWest) from the five routeMsg instances. It produces a single output drive event (o_drive*) and the corresponding message payload (o_*Msg_51). The arbMsg also receives the input free signal (i_free*) for its output direction, indicating that the downstream node is ready to accept a message.

claims.summary: Each directional port uses a three-signal handshake: a drive event to indicate a valid message, a 51-bit message payload, and a free signal to indicate readiness to accept the next message.
claims.subject: event-payload-free handshake per direction
claims.explanation: The event_payload_contracts show that each input drive event (i_drive*) is paired with an input message payload (i_*InMsg_51) and an output free signal (o_free*). Similarly, each output drive event (o_drive*) is paired with an output message payload (o_*Msg_51) and an input free signal (i_free*). This is a standard credit-based or ready/valid handshake for NoC routers, where the free signal acts as a credit or backpressure mechanism.

claims.summary: The five directional ports (East, Local, North, South, West) are symmetric in their interface signals and internal processing, indicating a homogeneous router design.
claims.subject: symmetric 5-port NoC router interface
claims.explanation: Each direction has identical sets of input/output drive events, input/output message payloads, and input/output free signals. The internal structure is also symmetric: each direction has a routeMsg instance and an arbMsg instance. This symmetry simplifies documentation and indicates that the router treats all directions equally.

claims.summary: The manual should emphasize the two-stage pipeline: routeMsg decodes the destination and generates requests, then arbMsg selects one request per output.
claims.subject: route-then-arbitrate pipeline
claims.explanation: The key component connections show a clear separation: routeMsg instances produce requests to all arbMsg instances, and arbMsg instances select one. This is the core architectural pattern of the nodeTop module. The documentation should explain how routing decisions are made in routeMsg and how arbitration is performed in arbMsg.

claims.summary: The manual should explain the free signal flow, where input free signals go to arbMsg instances and output free signals come from routeMsg instances, as a credit-based backpressure mechanism.
claims.subject: free signal backpressure flow
claims.explanation: The free signals are not simply forwarded. Input free signals (i_free*) go to arbMsg instances, indicating that the downstream node for that output direction is ready. Output free signals (o_free*) come from routeMsg instances, indicating that the routeMsg has completed processing and is ready for the next message. This is a key aspect of the handshake protocol.
